feedback.message: Not yet — `speak` is inherited from Animal, but the object is a Dog. Which `sound` does dynamic dispatch choose?

hints: The variable's declared type is Animal; the object's run-time class is Dog.
Instance method calls, including `sound()` inside `speak()`, are dispatched on the run-time class.
exercises.solution: It prints **`I say woof`**. `speak()` is inherited from Animal, but inside it the call `sound()` means `this.sound()`, and `this` is a Dog, so Dog's override runs. This is exactly how the template method in the Sensor example works.

feedback.message: Not yet — static methods are not dispatched on the object. Which type does the compiler see for `x`?
Not yet — `me()` is an instance method that B overrides, and the object is a B.

hints: Static calls are resolved at compile time from the declared type of the expression.
Instance calls are resolved at run time from the object's class.
exercises.solution: It prints **`AB`**. `x` is declared as `A`, and static methods are bound at compile time by that declared type, so `x.who()` calls `A.who()`; B's `who` only *hides* it. `x.me()` is an instance method, dispatched on the object's run-time class B. Write `A.who()` or `B.who()` explicitly to avoid this confusion.

feedback.message: Not yet — that is `inc.twice()` applied once. `twice()` is called twice, so the original operation runs four times.
Not yet — `twice` composes the operation with itself; it does not multiply by anything.

hints: `inc.twice()` adds 3 two times, so it adds 6.
Calling `twice()` on that adds 6 two times.
exercises.solution: `inc` adds 3. `inc.twice()` is a new Op that applies `inc` twice, adding 6. `.twice()` again applies *that* twice, adding 12. Starting from 1 gives **13**. Inside the default method, `apply` refers to the abstract method of whichever Op `twice` was called on, which is how the lambda captures the original behaviour.

exercises.prompt: Given `static double total(List<? extends Number> numbers)`, which arguments compile? Choose all that apply.

options.label: A `List<Integer>`
options.feedback: Yes. Integer is a subtype of Number.

options.label: A `List<Double>`
options.feedback: Yes. Double is a subtype of Number.

options.label: A `List<Number>`
options.feedback: Yes. `? extends Number` includes Number itself.

options.label: A `List<Object>`
options.feedback: Not yet — Object is a supertype of Number, not a subtype. That would need `? super Number`.

options.label: A `List<String>`
options.feedback: Not yet — String is not a Number at all.

hints: `? extends Number` means "some unknown type that is Number or a subtype of Number".
exercises.solution: **a**, **b** and **c**. The wildcard accepts any list whose element type is Number or a subtype. Inside `total` you can read each element as a Number, which is all the method needs. You could not add to the list, because the method does not know whether it holds Integers, Doubles or something else.

exercises.prompt: You are writing `static void fillWithZeros(List<___> target, int n)`, which adds `n` Integer zeros to `target`. Which declaration lets callers pass a `List<Integer>`, a `List<Number>` or a `List<Object>`?

options.label: `List<? super Integer>`
options.feedback: Yes. The list consumes Integers, so any list whose element type is Integer or a supertype is safe.

options.label: `List<? extends Integer>`
options.feedback: Not yet — with `extends` you cannot add anything except null, because the exact element type is unknown.

options.label: `List<Integer>`
options.feedback: Not yet — generic types are invariant, so this rejects List<Number> and List<Object>.

options.label: `List<Object>`
options.feedback: Not yet — invariance again: a List<Integer> is not a List<Object>.

hints: PECS: producer extends, consumer super. Does `target` produce values for you, or consume values you give it?
exercises.solution: **`List<? super Integer>`**. The method only *puts* Integers into the list, so the list is a consumer, and any list that can hold an Integer (Integer, Number, Object) qualifies. With `extends` you could read but not add; with an exact type you would accept only one of the three.

exercises.prompt: Inside `class Holder<T>`, which of these does the compiler **reject** because of type erasure? Choose all that apply.

options.label: `return new T();`
options.feedback: Rejected: at run time the JVM does not know what T is, so it cannot construct one.

options.label: `return new T[10];`
options.feedback: Rejected: "generic array creation". An array must know its element class at run time.

options.label: `return o instanceof T;`
options.feedback: Rejected: there is no T at run time to test against.

options.label: `List<T> items = new ArrayList<>();`
options.feedback: Not yet — this is fine. The compiler checks the type argument, and at run time it is simply an ArrayList.

hints: Ask of each line: does it need to know the actual class of T while the program is running?
exercises.solution: **a**, **b** and **c** are rejected; **d** is ordinary generic code. Generics are checked at compile time and then erased, so anything that needs T's actual class at run time (creating a T, creating a T[], testing `instanceof T`) cannot work. The standard workarounds are to pass a `Supplier<T>` or a `Class<T>` into the constructor, and to use lists instead of arrays.
